stem: Which statement defines the potential difference between two points in a circuit?

options.content: The energy transferred to other forms per unit time between the two points
options.rationale: Energy per unit time is power.

options.content: The energy transferred to other forms per unit charge passing between them
options.rationale: Correct: V = W/Q.

options.content: The charge that flows per unit time between the points
options.rationale: Charge per unit time is current.

options.content: The force acting on each unit of charge placed between the two points
options.rationale: Force per unit charge is electric field strength.

explanation: The p.d. is the energy transferred from electrical to other forms per unit charge passing between the two points: V = W/Q.

stem: Which is the volt expressed in SI base units?

options.rationale: This divides the joule by the ampere only; a coulomb is A s.
The ampere should be in the denominator: V = P/I.
This uses the newton instead of the joule (a metre is missing).
Correct: J C⁻¹ = kg m² s⁻² ÷ (A s).

explanation: $\text{V} = \text{J C}^{-1} = \dfrac{\text{kg m}^2\,\text{s}^{-2}}{\text{A s}} = \text{kg m}^2\,\text{s}^{-3}\,\text{A}^{-1}$. Equivalently $\text{V} = \text{W A}^{-1}$.

stem: Resistors of $4.0\ \Omega$ and $12\ \Omega$ are connected in parallel across a battery. What is the ratio $\dfrac{\text{power in the } 4.0\ \Omega \text{ resistor}}{\text{power in the } 12\ \Omega \text{ resistor}}$?

options.rationale: This uses P = I²R with equal currents, but parallel resistors have equal p.d., not equal current.
The ratio of resistances is not squared: P ∝ 1/R at fixed V.
The p.d. is the same, but the powers are not.
Correct: same V, so P = V²/R and P ∝ 1/R.

explanation: In parallel both have the same p.d. $V$. $P = V^2/R$, so $\dfrac{P_4}{P_{12}} = \dfrac{12}{4.0} = 3$: the smaller resistor dissipates more power.
hints: What is the same for resistors in parallel?

stem: A heater of constant resistance is rated $1500\ \text{W}$ at $230\ \text{V}$. During a period of low mains voltage the supply falls to $200\ \text{V}$. What is the power of the heater now?

options.rationale: Correct: P = V²/R with R unchanged, so P ∝ V².
This assumes P ∝ V; with constant R, P ∝ V².
The rated power applies only at the rated voltage.
This inverts the ratio; the power must fall when the voltage falls.

hints: Find the resistance from the rating.

stem: Two lamps, P and Q, are connected in series to a battery. The resistance of P is twice that of Q. Which statement is correct?

options.content: Q dissipates twice the power of P.
options.rationale: That would be true in parallel (same V), not in series.

options.content: P dissipates twice the power of Q.
options.rationale: Correct: same current, so P = I²R ∝ R.

options.content: P and Q dissipate equal power because they share the same current.
options.rationale: Equal current does not mean equal power when the resistances differ.

options.content: P dissipates four times the power of Q.
options.rationale: Power is proportional to R at fixed current, not to R².

explanation: In series the current is the same in both lamps. P = I²R, so the lamp with twice the resistance dissipates twice the power.

stem: When $450\ \text{C}$ of charge passes through a motor, $5.4\ \text{kJ}$ of energy is transferred. What is the p.d. across the motor?

options.rationale: Correct: V = W/Q.
This multiplies energy and charge instead of dividing.
This divides charge by energy (inverted).
This forgets to convert kJ to J.

stem: An immersion heater has a resistance of $20\ \Omega$ and carries a current of $11\ \text{A}$. Calculate its power, in W.
explanation: $P = I^2R = 11^2 \times 20 = 2420\ \text{W}$. Using $P = IR$ forgets the square.
workedSolution: 1. $P = I^2R = 11^2 \times 20 = 2420\ \text{W}$. Using $P = IR$ forgets the square.

stem: A car's interior lamp is rated $6.0\ \text{V}$, $9.0\ \text{W}$ (the lamp runs from a low-voltage supply). Calculate its resistance at its working temperature, in Ω.

A $1.2\ \text{kW}$ borehole pump runs for $3.5$ hours every day for 31 days. Electricity costs US\$0.14 per kW h (illustrative). Calculate the cost of running the pump for the month, in US dollars, to two decimal places.
explanation:
1. Energy $= 1.2\ \text{kW} \times 3.5\ \text{h} \times 31 = 130.2\ \text{kW h}$.
2. Cost $= 130.2 \times 0.14 =$ US\$18.23.
3. Using 1200 (watts) instead of 1.2 kW gives a cost 1000 times too large.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Energy $= 1.2\ \text{kW} \times 3.5\ \text{h} \times 31 = 130.2\ \text{kW h}$.
2. Cost $= 130.2 \times 0.14 =$ US\$18.23.
3. Using 1200 (watts) instead of 1.2 kW gives a cost 1000 times too large.
hints: Energy in kW h = power in kW × time in hours.

stem: A $60\ \text{W}$ television is left on for 8.0 hours. Calculate the energy transferred, in MJ, to three significant figures.
explanation: $W = Pt = 60 \times (8.0 \times 3600) = 1.73 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J} = 1.73\ \text{MJ}$ (that is $0.48\ \text{kW h}$).

stem: A workshop $45\ \text{m}$ from a house is supplied through a two-core cable; each core has a resistance of $0.0072\ \Omega$ per metre. A $230\ \text{V}$ supply at the house drives a current of $18\ \text{A}$ to a maize mill motor. Calculate the p.d. across the motor, in V, to three significant figures.
explanation:
1. The current travels out and back: cable length $= 2 \times 45 = 90\ \text{m}$; $R_{\text{cable}} = 90 \times 0.0072 = 0.648\ \Omega$.
2. P.d. lost in the cable $= IR = 18 \times 0.648 = 11.7\ \text{V}$.
3. P.d. across the motor $= 230 - 11.7 = 218\ \text{V}$.
4. The cable also wastes $I^2R = 210\ \text{W}$. Using only one core (45 m) halves the loss wrongly.
workedSolution:
1. 1. The current travels out and back: cable length $= 2 \times 45 = 90\ \text{m}$; $R_{\text{cable}} = 90 \times 0.0072 = 0.648\ \Omega$.
2. P.d. lost in the cable $= IR = 18 \times 0.648 = 11.7\ \text{V}$.
3. P.d. across the motor $= 230 - 11.7 = 218\ \text{V}$.
4. The cable also wastes $I^2R = 210\ \text{W}$. Using only one core (45 m) halves the loss wrongly.
hints: Both cores carry the current: double the length.
Lost volts = I × R of the cable.

stem: An urn heats $1.5\ \text{kg}$ of water (specific heat capacity $4200\ \text{J kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$) from $25\ ^\circ\text{C}$ to $95\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Its element is rated $2.4\ \text{kW}$ and 90% of the electrical energy goes into the water. Calculate the heating time, in s, to three significant figures.
explanation:
1. Energy needed by the water $= mc\Delta\theta = 1.5 \times 4200 \times 70 = 4.41 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$.
2. Useful power $= 0.90 \times 2400 = 2160\ \text{W}$.
3. $t = \dfrac{4.41 \times 10^{5}}{2160} = 204\ \text{s}$ (about 3.4 minutes).
4. Ignoring the efficiency gives too short a time.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Energy needed by the water $= mc\Delta\theta = 1.5 \times 4200 \times 70 = 4.41 \times 10^{5}\ \text{J}$.
2. Useful power $= 0.90 \times 2400 = 2160\ \text{W}$.
3. $t = \dfrac{4.41 \times 10^{5}}{2160} = 204\ \text{s}$ (about 3.4 minutes).
4. Ignoring the efficiency gives too short a time.
hints: Only 90% of the power heats the water.

stem: Name the unit equal to one joule per coulomb.
explanation: The **volt**: 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.

stem: Explain why electrical energy is transmitted over long distances at a high voltage rather than at a low voltage.

points.description: For a given power P = VI, a higher voltage means a smaller current.
Power lost as heat in the cables is I²R.
So a smaller current greatly reduces the energy wasted (the loss falls with the square of the current); thinner, cheaper cables can be used.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: To deliver a given power P = VI, a higher voltage needs a smaller current. The power wasted in the line is I²R, which depends on the square of the current, so the losses are much smaller at high voltage, and lighter, cheaper conductors can be used.

explanation: P = VI fixes the current for a given power; losses are I²R.
hints: Which formula gives the power lost in the cables?

stem: Show that the power dissipated in a resistor of resistance $R$ with p.d. $V$ across it is $V^2/R$, starting from the definition of potential difference.

points.description: $V = W/Q$, so energy $W = VQ$; with $Q = It$, $W = VIt$.
$R = V/I$ gives $I = V/R$, so $P = V \times V/R = V^2/R$.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: From the definition, $W = VQ = VIt$, so $P = W/t = VI$. Since $I = V/R$, $P = V^2/R$.

explanation: Combine V = W/Q, Q = It and R = V/I.

stem: Rudo says: 'A 100 W lamp is always brighter than a 60 W lamp.' The two filament lamps, both rated for 230 V, are connected in series across a 230 V supply. Explain which lamp is brighter and comment on her statement.

points.description: Using R = V²/P at the rated values, the 60 W lamp has the larger resistance.
In series the current is the same in both lamps.
P = I²R, so the 60 W lamp (larger R) dissipates more power and is brighter.
So her statement is only true when each lamp works at its rated p.d. (e.g. in parallel); ratings apply at the rated voltage.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: From R = V²/P, the 60 W lamp has the higher resistance. In series both lamps carry the same current, and P = I²R, so the 60 W lamp dissipates more power and glows brighter. Rudo is right only when each lamp has its rated 230 V across it, as in parallel. (The filament resistances change with temperature, but the 60 W lamp still has the larger resistance.)

explanation: Series: same I, so the larger R gives the larger I²R.
hints: Which lamp has the larger resistance?
What is common to lamps in series?
